summary.title: Écluse
summary.description: STRIDE threat model for Écluse, a supply-chain policy proxy for package registries. The 'High Level' diagram captures the canonical deployment posture. It shows per-caller passthrough credentials and AWS CodeArtifact reached over VPC endpoints. The three registries are a first-party private store, a public-derived mirror store, and a pull-through read endpoint. The demand-driven mirror worker mints its own write token under the container role. Edge access control and storage-layer scanning are operator responsibilities and out of scope, recorded as trust assumptions. This model is an iterative sketch, refined collaboratively. The .json file is the single source of truth, and Threat Dragon renders it.

label.text: Operator trust zone (VPC / mesh): access edge enforced here

data.name:
npm client
(developer / CI)
data.description: The caller. It presents its own CodeArtifact bearer token. The operator's access edge authenticates it to the proxy, not Écluse.

data.name: Public npm registry
data.description: The upstream registry. Its tarball bytes and author-supplied manifest fields are untrusted. The rules engine and the integrity floor gate them, and Écluse never serves them blindly. Écluse trusts the fields the registry itself asserts only to the floor that the registry operator is honest. The per-version publish time is server-stamped, and so is server-side integrity. npm, PyPI, and RubyGems record the publish time server-side, and it is absent from the publish document, so a publisher cannot backdate it. A compromised or malicious registry operator that forged those fields sits below this necessary trust floor and is out of scope. Écluse queries the registry anonymously, with the caller credential stripped.

threats.title: Upstream registry forges its own server-asserted metadata (e.g. a backdated publish time)
threats.description: Écluse's freshness quarantine and integrity reasoning consume fields the upstream registry asserts, notably the per-version publish time and server-side integrity. A registry that asserted forged values could admit content the age and integrity gates would otherwise hold back. A backdated time defeats the age quarantine, and a manufactured digest defeats the integrity check.
threats.mitigation: Risk treatment: accepted by trust assumption. The primary registries stamp these fields server-side. The publish time is not part of the publish document, so a publisher cannot forge it. Écluse reads the registry's metadata, so it necessarily extends a floor of trust to the registry operator's honesty. A hostile operator is an adversary this model cannot counter, the same class as 'what if npm itself is malicious'. What is untrusted here are the tarball contents and the author-supplied fields, and the rules engine and the integrity floor do gate those. The freshness quarantine's age signal depends on the upstream's timestamp honesty, so a registry that asserted a forged time could in theory defeat it. Écluse could re-anchor age to its own first observation of a version and remove that dependence. It deliberately does not. The central public registries, npmjs and PyPI among them, are foundational to modern software infrastructure. Trusting their server-stamped timestamps is the only practical recourse. A dependable first-observation anchor would need durable, replica-shared state, at odds with Écluse's network-broker design. It would also narrow only a surface that already sits outside the practical treatment boundary. Écluse records this as accepted residual risk rather than mitigated.

data.name: AWS IMDS + STS
data.description: Instance-metadata and token endpoint. It sources the container-role credentials the worker exchanges for a CodeArtifact write token. Écluse reaches it over amazonka's own client, off the guarded data-plane manager.

data.name: Écluse proxy
data.description: The request pipeline: router, parallel upstream fetch, packument merge, deny-by-default rules and integrity gate, then serve. It relays publishes. It holds forwarded caller credentials transiently. It polls S3 for OSV db updates and performs an atomic shadow-swap for CVE boundaries.

threats.title: Forwarded caller credentials aggregated in proxy memory
threats.description: Under the canonical passthrough strategy the proxy transiently holds every caller's own CodeArtifact bearer token in process memory while it relays reads and publishes. One proxy compromise therefore harvests the credentials of all callers in transit, not one. A heap or memory dump, a log-field leak, and a malicious dependency in Écluse's own supply chain all reach that result. Passthrough spreads credential exposure across every user. A service identity would instead concentrate it in one short-lived token.
threats.mitigation: Écluse carries a token in a redacted type, the Secret newtype, whose Show renders a fixed placeholder, so a token never reaches a log field. Retention is request-scoped, and the code unwraps a token only at the point of use, to attach the bearer to an outbound request. Neither the data-plane nor the WAI span instrumentation records an Authorization header, so a credential never reaches a span. The WAI layer does record benign request headers, such as User-Agent. A regression test holds the split. Residual: a garbage-collected runtime cannot guarantee prompt erasure from the heap. The first-class compensating control is therefore hardening Écluse's own runtime and supply chain, through the attested, reproducible image that the image vulnerability-scan gate keeps clean.

threats.title: Chokepoint exhaustion via pathological upstream payload
threats.description: Écluse is a mandatory chokepoint, so degrading its availability is itself a supply-chain attack. Builds fail, or operators are tempted to bypass the gate. A hostile or compromised upstream registry, or a pathological public package, could return an oversized, version-flooded, or deeply nested packument. Parsing it and evaluating the rules per version could then exhaust CPU or memory.
threats.mitigation: Fail-closed caps bound the input: body size, version count, artifact count, and nesting depth (ECLUSE_LIMITS__MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES, ECLUSE_LIMITS__MAX_VERSION_COUNT, ECLUSE_LIMITS__MAX_ARTIFACT_COUNT, ECLUSE_LIMITS__MAX_NESTING_DEPTH). The bounded read stops mid-stream. The serve path is O(n log n) in version count, a Map-based merge with no super-linear blow-up. The single-flight cache coalesces concurrent misses for the same package onto one computation, and a per-request timeout caps any single request. Écluse still projects the whole document before the version cap rejects it. Failing fast at the cap is an accepted residual for v0.1.0. The advisory-backed rules compound that cost. They evaluate each version on its own, with no memoisation, and take one or two advisory lookups per version, so a near-cap document multiplies those lookups. Batching them per package is required to remove the amplification. Resident-bytes and serve-concurrency admission bounds further cap the aggregate resident cost. The residual is resource amplification, not algorithmic complexity. A near-cap document still costs real CPU and heap, and distinct-key floods bypass single-flight, worst under a hostile or compromised upstream registry. Volumetric and concurrency rate-limiting is therefore an operator-edge responsibility, as access control is.

threats.title: Proxy compromised via tampered OSV database
threats.description: An attacker who can write to the S3 bucket could supply a tampered osv.db and bypass the vulnerability gates. Worse, they could exploit memory-corruption bugs in the underlying C SQLite engine when the proxy runs a query. A Magellan-style exploit or a malicious trigger is the vector.
threats.mitigation: The S3 bucket is private, and the proxy's IAM role holds GetObject only. An atomic shadow-swap prevents a partial read. The proxy binds the SQLite connection to read-only mode and disables trusted schema (PRAGMA trusted_schema = OFF;) as it opens the connection. An attacker-controlled trigger or view therefore never runs. Acceptance then verifies the artifact before the proxy serves it: the schema epoch stamp, a PRAGMA quick_check integrity walk, the required tables, and the ecosystem. The quick_check walk also verifies stored values against each STRICT table's declared column types. The required tables must be real STRICT tables carrying the required columns. Acceptance refuses a failing artifact as a rejection value, remembers its ETag, and keeps the last-good database serving.

data.name: Mirror worker
data.description: The demand-driven asynchronous worker. It polls the mirror queue, back-fills the approved artifact from the upstream registry, and verifies the bytes against dist.integrity. It then publishes to the mirror store with Écluse's own minted write token.

data.name: Credential provider
data.description: It holds each mirroring mount's write credential for that mount's mirror target, built from the store the target's tag names. A CodeArtifact store mints and refreshes a short-lived token under the container or task role, with single-flight and a breaker, and identities that coincide share one provider. Every other store carries the operator's static token. This is Écluse's only standing credential.

data.name:
Metadata cache
(public-gated only)
data.description: The shared in-proxy cache. It holds only the anonymous public gated origin. Écluse never enters the per-caller private origin, under any strategy.

threats.title: Cross-client disclosure of a private package via shared cache (#115)
threats.description: A cache key carries no credential dimension. If the cache held a private-origin document, one caller could warm an entry and a second, differently authorised caller could receive it. That second caller receives the document without the upstream ever authorising their own request.
threats.mitigation: Écluse never enters the private origin into the shared cache. Module encapsulation is the guarantee: the cache-entering client builder is unexported, and the private-origin path hard-codes an uncached fetch. The cache holds only the anonymous public-gated origin. Écluse re-consults the private origin on every request, with the caller's own forwarded token. The cache-recovering designs that would share a private entry, delegated-cache and memoised, are rejected by design. No shared private cache exists to leak.

data.name: Mirror queue (SQS)
data.description: The demand-driven mirror job queue. Écluse enqueues a job when it accepts an artifact on the tarball path. The queue is a trusted, operator-declared destination, reached over amazonka's own client.

data.name:
Registry C:
pull-through read endpoint
data.description: The trusted private-upstream read view, declared under the mount's `privateUpstream` with the tag that names its store. It is a pull-through aggregator over the first-party store (A) and the mirror store (B), and it is what the proxy reads.

threats.title: Undetected artifact substitution across upstreams
threats.description: The merge flags an integrity divergence when the private and public copies of a version contradict on a shared digest algorithm. A weak-only or absent digest could let a substituted artifact pass undetected and reach the client as the trusted copy. So could a flaw in the divergence key.
threats.mitigation: Écluse admits a public version only if it carries a digest that meets the integrity floor: a uniform SHA-256 default, hard-floored. Divergence compares each digest's asserted algorithm, not a bucketed tag. The merge detects a real same-version contradiction on a shared algorithm, and the serve path consumes it. Écluse logs it at WARNING, naming the package, the contradicting versions, and their digests, and meters it as ecluse.registry.merge.divergence. A substitution therefore surfaces, and the merge never silently reconciles it. The trusted copy always wins the served bytes. The operator's ECLUSE_INTEGRITY__DIVERGENCE_POLICY then decides whether Écluse also withholds the contested version from the listing (fail-closed) or serves it with the alarm (warn, the default). Residual: warn detects without withholding, so an operator who wants prevention rather than detection must set fail-closed. The trusted-floor path is deliberately operator-loosenable, trading strictness for availability, and that is the remaining way a weak digest is accepted. A serve-only mount with no private upstream, the pure public gate, has a single origin, so cross-upstream divergence detection is structurally absent. That is an accepted residual of that sub-shape. A serve-only mount that reads a private upstream keeps the detection unchanged.

threats.title: Private-upstream aggregation admits the public registry, bypassing the gate
threats.description: The recommended topology unions the trusted stores, first-party A and the sanitised mirror B, into the pull-through read endpoint C at the registry level. CodeArtifact upstream relationships are one such mechanism. If that aggregation also holds a direct connection to the upstream registry, raw public packages reach clients through C as a trusted source. They skip Écluse's gate entirely: the rules, the integrity floor, and the freshness quarantine. The same upstream-merger mechanism that makes the ideal topology work makes this the natural misconfiguration. A CodeArtifact repository's default npm-store upstream to npmjs is exactly this shape.
threats.mitigation: The control is an operator-architecture invariant, documented in the registry model and the Golden Path. The aggregating private upstream composes trusted stores only, first-party plus Écluse's sanitised mirror, and never carries a direct public upstream. Public content enters only through Écluse's gate. Écluse cannot detect a violation: the private upstream is trusted by construction, and its upstream wiring sits outside the proxy. The control is therefore operator discipline and this documented invariant, not a structural check.

data.name:
Registry A:
private store (first-party)
data.description: First-party and internal packages, written by a client npm publish under passthrough. Écluse trusts this store and serves it unfiltered. It is the publication target.

data.name:
Registry B:
mirror store (public-derived)
data.description: Public packages that the rules approved and the worker replicated. It is the mirror target. It stays distinct from A so first-party and public-derived inventory remain separable.

threats.title: Registry collapse erases provenance and per-store policy
threats.description: Écluse supports collapsing its internal registry roles onto as few as one store. The recommended topology keeps the first-party store (A) and the public-derived mirror store (B) separate. It then unions them into the pull-through read endpoint (C) at the registry level. Collapsing them onto a single shared store is the degenerate floor. An undeclared mounts.<eco>.mirrorTarget makes the mount serve-only, with no mirror store at all. The fold is a mirrorTarget set equal to the private upstream, which the boot warns about and then accepts. Collapse loses the physical separation between first-party and public-derived inventory. Distinct storage-level rule sets and scanning per provenance become impossible. Collapse also muddies post-disclosure incident scoping, 'which mirrored public packages did we hold?', which weakens the arithmetic-not-forensics response.
threats.mitigation: Deploy the recommended three-registry topology, the Golden Path: a first-party store, a public-derived mirror store, and a pull-through aggregator read endpoint. The endpoint unions the other two at the registry level. Each of the three is independently governable. The single-registry collapse stays supported but discouraged. It trades auditability and defence in depth, not the perimeter. An operator who deliberately chooses a collapsed topology accepts that local residual risk against their own threat tolerance.

threats.title: Malicious mirrored version persists and is served as trusted (no automatic post-ingestion revocation)
threats.description: Écluse mirrors approved public versions into Registry B and, by design, resists upstream yanks so a benign yank does not break installs. The cost is that a version later found malicious persists in B and is served as trusted. The merge serves the private origin unfiltered by the rules. Nothing removes it automatically: neither an upstream yank nor a rules change reaches an already-mirrored artifact.
threats.mitigation: The freshness quarantine (`AllowIfOlderThan`) is the primary defence. It delays serving a new version until advisories have time to surface, so the rules deny most malicious versions at admission, before any mirroring. This threat is the residual for a version found bad after it cleared the quarantine and was mirrored. Detection is delegated: operator scanning of Registry B, upstream advisories, and security-holding signals decide what to revoke. Enforcement is layered across the version's lifecycle. The hard deny-by-identity rule (DenyByIdentity) halts re-admission on the serve path and re-mirroring at the worker's ingest re-check. That is the immediate, surgical stop, and it also breaks the re-mirror treadmill. An automated reaper, the Écluse Dredger, must continually prune already-mirrored versions that the shared rules engine now denies, on a named decisive deny that is advisory-driven or identity-driven and never an age condition, so recovery follows a public alert without an operator step. It is required to run as a separate service that shares the core rules engine and exposes only its liveness and readiness probes. The operator can also purge a version from Registry B directly. The rules never run on trusted content, so a purge is what removes the already-mirrored copy. Order the two as deny then purge, so demand does not re-mirror during the purge. A purge alone is a treadmill while the version is still live upstream. The typical pattern is the inverse. An upstream yank or security hold removes or changes the bytes first. Re-mirroring then cannot reproduce them, and a purge clears the stale copy. Irreducible residual: a malicious version with no public advisory cannot be reaped, because there is nothing to detect on. That is the bound the freshness quarantine exists to provide. Retained pull-through copies in the private upstream can outlive removal from the mirror, and their safe removal is future work pending verification against a real deployment. A serve-only mount has no trusted store of mirrored versions at all. Every serve re-gates under current policy, so a rules change or a fresh advisory takes effect immediately. This threat's surface exists only where a mirrorTarget is declared.

data.name: npm read / publish (passthrough CodeArtifact token)
data.description: The caller's request, carrying its own CodeArtifact bearer token. It crosses the operator access edge.

threats.title: Off-by-default edge auth assumes a sound network boundary
threats.description: The edge token, server.authToken (ECLUSE_SERVER__AUTH_TOKEN), is off by default. Écluse delegates 'who may reach the proxy' to the operator's access edge: a gateway, a mesh, or a network policy. If that boundary fails, an unauthenticated caller can drive the proxy. The east-west case is the notable one: a compromised neighbour reaches the pod directly and bypasses an ingress-only IP allow-list.
threats.mitigation: Compensating control: under passthrough the request carries only the caller's own forwarded token, and the read path never substitutes a standing credential. No forwarded token means no private read. A breach of the edge exposes only the public-gated view plus the untrusted-egress and denial-of-service surface, never private packages. The publish path is the one exception. A configured static publication-target credential (mounts.<eco>.publicationTarget.<tag>.token) serves as the fallback for a tokenless publish, so 'no token, no publish' holds only for pure passthrough. The internal-credential publish mode is therefore fail-closed by construction. A configured publication-target token requires a verifiable inbound edge, server.authToken or stronger, so the composition root refuses internal-credential-plus-open-edge at boot. That state is unrepresentable, on the same principle the trusted-edge read identity follows. Restrict both north-south and east-west access, as the Golden Path documents. Any edge mode that substitutes Écluse's own identity, read or write, must require a verifiable edge. Use mTLS or a shared secret, never a bare spoofable header.

threats.title: Package-name spoofing via invisible characters
threats.description: A requested or published package name can impersonate another package to a human reader. Unicode format characters (zero-width and bidirectional controls) render invisibly or reorder glyphs, so two distinct names look identical in a lockfile, a log line, or a review diff. A name can arrive from an upstream fetch as well as from a first-party publish, so the boundary applies to both directions.
threats.mitigation: Every package-name component parses against an explicit ASCII allowlist before routing, caching, queueing, or publish admission. For npm the allowlist is the validator's own hard boundary: letters, digits, and - _ . ! ~ * ' ( ), with @ and / as scope structure and no leading period, hyphen, or underscore. A codepoint outside the set, non-ASCII or control, cannot enter by construction, on the serve path or the publish path.

threats.title: Package-name typosquatting within the permitted character set
threats.description: A name built only from permitted ASCII characters can read as another name to a human: a capital I in place of a lowercase l, rn in place of m, a swapped or doubled letter, a hyphen moved or dropped. The upstream npm namespace already contains such look-alike names, and a first-party publish can introduce one. A reader of a lockfile, a log line, or a review diff resolves the wrong package.
threats.mitigation: The ASCII allowlist bounds the space to visible permitted characters, which keeps every name renderable and comparable. Detection or refusal of look-alike names within the permitted set is not implemented.

data.name: read packument / tarball (caller token forwarded)
data.description: A per-request private read with the caller's own token. The upstream re-authorises each request. Écluse never shared-caches this read under passthrough.

data.name: cache public-gated metadata
data.description: Reads and writes of the anonymous public gated origin only.

data.name: anonymous packument / tarball fetch (caller token stripped)
data.description: Untrusted egress to the upstream registry. The target is attacker-influenceable, so Écluse strips the caller credential. The flow crosses to the public internet and is forced HTTPS-only.

threats.title: Caller credential leak to the public upstream
threats.description: The upstream registry is attacker-influenceable and must never receive a caller's credential. A failure to strip the caller token on the public fetch would disclose a live CodeArtifact token to public npm. So would following a cross-host 3xx with the bearer still attached, to an attacker-chosen redirect target, over the unguarded private manager.
threats.mitigation: Écluse strips the caller credential before every public fetch and queries the registry anonymously. A credential-bearing request never follows a redirect: the shared parse entry seals every request it hands back with redirectCount=0, and the credential attach re-applies that seal, so no adapter can obtain an unpinned request. That matters because the http-client in use does not drop Authorization on a cross-host redirect.

threats.title: SSRF via crafted identifier or upstream-declared dist.tarball
threats.description: Écluse builds outbound URLs from client-supplied package identifiers and upstream-declared artifact locations. A traversal, encoded-slash, or absolute-URL name could steer a fetch to an unintended target such as cloud metadata or the private network. So could a dist.tarball that points at an internal or attacker-chosen host.
threats.mitigation: Écluse canonicalises the identifier and encodes on build. It also enforces an outbound host and port allow-list, the load-bearing control, where it builds the request URL. Registry egress is https-only by construction. Every outbound registry URL goes through a typed boundary, mkRegistryUrl, which rejects any non-https scheme, and a non-https configured endpoint fails closed at boot. TLS certificate validation authenticates the dialled host. A name steered to an internal or rebound address cannot present a CA-trusted certificate for the requested host. Certificate validation therefore closes the resolve-to-internal and DNS-rebinding SSRF class, rather than a resolved-IP recheck. No data-plane request follows an upstream redirect, because the shared parse entry pins redirectCount=0 on every request it returns and the mirror-write transport re-pins whatever an adapter's codec forms. No redirect hop can escape the build-time allow-list or downgrade the scheme. A disallow-by-default same-authority policy applies to every upstream-declared artifact location, matched on host and port, with the hosts an ecosystem serves artifact bytes from by design as its one equivalence. Écluse upgrades a legacy http location to https on the same host, and drops and records a file the scheme or the authority refuses. The projection and the download gate read one definition of that authority check, so a refused file is absent from the served listing rather than listed and refused at download, and a release drops when no file of it survives. The trusted private origin meets the same https requirement. A cheap pure literal internal-range block remains as defence in depth on the artifact-host gate. An operator can extend that fixed range set with ECLUSE_EGRESS__ADDITIONAL_BLOCKED_RANGES for internal space the module cannot know in advance. That setting is widen-only and fails closed at boot on a malformed entry.

threats.title: Connect-time reachability/timing oracle for an attacker-controlled allowlisted DNS
threats.description: An attacker who controls the DNS for an allowlisted host can repoint it at internal addresses. https-only egress with certificate validation makes the TLS handshake fail, because an internal address cannot present a CA-trusted certificate for the requested host. Écluse therefore sends no request and leaks no data. The success or failure and the timing of the TCP connect and the TLS handshake are still a coarse internal-reachability or port-scan oracle.
threats.mitigation: Risk treatment: accepted residual. No data crosses the boundary: the connection fails at the TLS handshake, before any request body goes out. The surface covers only allowlisted hosts whose DNS the attacker already controls, and the signal is coarse, connect and handshake timing alone. The host allowlist bounds which names can be aimed inward at all. It does not remove the residual timing signal.

threats.title: Dependency confusion through a first-party namespace on the public upstream
threats.description: A mount declares the namespaces the deployment owns. An attacker registers a package on the public upstream under a name, scope, or prefix inside one of them, choosing a name the private store does not carry, or a version of one it does. Without the privilege the public leg would answer for that name: the packument merge would fold the public document in, the artifact path would stream its bytes after a private miss, and the mirror would write the admitted version into the deployment's own store. A build resolving a first-party dependency would install the attacker's package. That is dependency confusion, and the public leg is where it enters.
threats.mitigation: A first-party name has one authority, the private upstream. The composition root derives one predicate from the mount's declaration and hands the same value to every consumer, so no two of them can disagree about which names are privileged. The packument pipeline fetches the private origin alone for such a name, so no public document is fetched and none can be merged. The artifact pipeline ends a private miss there rather than falling through to the public leg. Nothing first-party is mirrored, because the mirror only enqueues a version the public leg admitted. A private miss is a 404, so no public package stands in for one the deployment owns. The declaration is parsed once at load into a closed per-ecosystem sum: npm matches a scope exactly, so @acme-evil does not satisfy @acme, and PyPI matches a PEP 503 canonical name exactly or a canonical prefix that stops at the separator, so acme-* covers acme-tools and not acmeco. An empty list is refused at load. Residual: a namespace the deployment has not declared carries no privilege, and a name the deployment owns but does not publish privately is unreachable rather than served from public.

data.name: relay npm publish (publisher token forwarded)
data.description: A first-party publish relayed to the private store with the publisher's own token. The mount's first-party namespaces gate it before any write.

threats.title: Package shadowing via first-party publish
threats.description: Écluse relays a publish to the private store with the publisher's own token. The packument merge serves private versions as trusted, winning collisions over public ones. A compromised-CI or insider publisher could clear the first-party check, or slip past it. They could then publish a name that the merge serves as a trusted version over the public package. That is a dependency-confusion path through Écluse's own trust model.
threats.mitigation: The mount's firstParty declaration, for npm a list of scopes, refuses any name outside the namespaces the deployment owns before any upstream write. That is the anti-shadowing guard. The scope match is exact on the parsed namespace, so a prefix such as @acme-evil does not satisfy an @acme entry. Soundness requires the authorised identity to be the written identity. Écluse validates the publish document's own declared name and _id, and the per-version names, equal to the scope-guarded URL-path name before the relay. It then builds the write URL from that same canonical name. The guarded name, the written name, and the merge collision key are therefore one identity by construction. Residual: shadowing within a declared scope, and allow-precedence choices, stay the operator's risk. Give the publisher's target credential least privilege.

threats.title: Publisher credential relayed to a misdirected publication target
threats.description: The publish path forwards the publisher's own registry token to the operator-declared publication target. A publication target written by mistake, or edited to a wrong value, would send that live bearer credential to a registry the publisher never meant to authenticate to. A public registry is the worst case: an operator who points the publication target at the public upstream turns every publish into a credential disclosure to a third party that can log or replay it.
threats.mitigation: The publish path forwards the publisher's own credential only to the operator-declared publication target, and Écluse mints no token of its own for it. The boot refuses a publication target that shares a host with any mount's public upstream, and one that equals another mount's private upstream, mirror target, or publication target. The same host refusal covers a mirror target. Equality with its own mount's private upstream or mirror target stays legal, being the documented read-back topology. Only a vetted target reaches the relay: the value the publish binding carries is constructible only through that boot check. Credential-bearing requests never follow redirects, so no hop can move the write after the check. Every registry endpoint is https-only with certificate validation, so the credential reaches only a host holding a CA-trusted certificate for the declared name.

data.name: enqueue mirror job (demand-driven)
data.description: On tarball-path acceptance, Écluse enqueues a mirror job without blocking.

data.name: poll jobs
data.description: The worker polls the mirror queue for demand-driven jobs.

data.name: back-fill artifact fetch (untrusted)
data.description: The worker fetches the approved artifact from the upstream registry to mirror it. This is untrusted egress, forced HTTPS-only. The worker verifies the bytes against dist.integrity before it publishes.

threats.title: SSRF via the worker back-fill fetch (a blind sink)
threats.description: The mirror worker fetches the approved artifact from an upstream-declared dist.tarball location to replicate it. Like the serve-path public fetch, this is untrusted egress to an attacker-influenceable target. In principle it carries the same SSRF surface: a dist.tarball steered at an internal or cloud-metadata address.
threats.mitigation: The fetch runs on the same validating-TLS data-plane manager as the serve path. That manager gives https-only egress, certificate validation that authenticates the host, and the universal no-redirect invariant. The dist.tarball is https-only, and the outbound allow-list admitted the location host at serve time, before the job was enqueued. Decisively, this is a blind sink. The worker verifies the bytes against dist.integrity and publishes them. It never returns them to a caller. An internal or metadata response can present neither a CA-trusted certificate for the host nor a match for the asserted digest. The job therefore fails closed and is dropped rather than exfiltrating. Its impact sits well below the serve-path fetch. A serve-only mount enqueues no back-fill jobs, so this surface does not exist there.

data.name: request mirror-write token
data.description: The worker asks the credential provider for a mirror-target write token.

data.name: mint via container role (IMDSv2 / STS)
data.description: The credential provider exchanges container-role credentials for a CodeArtifact write token. It reaches an internal address by design.

threats.title: SSRF to the instance-metadata credential endpoint
threats.description: Container-role token minting must reach the instance-metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) and STS. An SSRF that reached metadata could mint the worker's CodeArtifact credential.
threats.mitigation: Écluse follows an internal-resolving location only on the trusted private origin, never on a client-influenced or upstream-influenced target. Nothing can therefore steer the data plane at metadata. Minting uses amazonka's own client, off the guarded data-plane manager. Operator defence in depth: require IMDSv2 and set the hop limit to 1. Do not block metadata outright.

data.name: publish mirrored artifact (minted write token)
data.description: The worker writes the verified, approved artifact to the mirror store with Écluse's own minted token.

threats.title: Mirror-write credential is a standing privilege over the trusted store
threats.description: The mirror worker holds Écluse's only standing self-minted credential. It carries write access to the mirror store (Registry B), which feeds the trusted read path. A worker compromise, or any bypass of the admission gate, could write attacker-chosen bytes into the trusted store and poison future reads.
threats.mitigation: Containment of this standing privilege rests on least privilege at the store. Under the `codeArtifact` tag the write token is minted from the container or task role and bears that role's own permissions, so containment is an access policy scoped write-only to the mirror store rather than a token-level scope, and the lifetime is short, capped by CodeArtifact at 12h. Under `registry` and `verdaccio` the write is the operator's static token, so containment is an account of the store's own: a dedicated user whose package rights cover the mirror store and nothing else. A store whose only control plane is the ecosystem protocol offers no split between writing and deleting, so on such a store this one credential also removes versions, and a compromise of the worker can empty the mirror as well as poison it. The publish runs with redirectCount=0, because the shared transport seals every request an adapter's codec returns, whether or not that codec routes through the credential attach. The mirror queue sits inside the same trust boundary and is isolated and managed at the infrastructure level. A job is unauthenticated data that directs the worker to fetch and publish, so queue-send access is equivalent to trusted-write access. Scope the queue's IAM so only the serve role enqueues (SendMessage) and only the worker receives and acks. Écluse relies on access control for message authenticity, deliberately, rather than on signatures. That is the standard pattern for an internal single-producer, single-consumer queue. The worker's own attack surface is small. It hashes the fetched bytes and forwards them unchanged, with no decompression and no tarball parsing. A malicious artifact is therefore a poor code-execution vector. The dist.integrity check is anti-tamper-in-transit and anti-downgrade. It fails closed when the strongest present digest is in an uncomputable algorithm, and never downgrades to a forgeable weaker one. It proves the bytes match the upstream's asserted digest, so it catches back-fill corruption but not a hostile upstream or a worker compromise. Admission-gate soundness therefore bounds the poisoning of future reads, together with the role's blast radius and queue access control, not the integrity check. The trusted store is only as clean as what the gate admits, and only the gate may enqueue. A serve-only mount, with no mirrorTarget declared, removes this surface entirely. It holds and mints no write credential, and with zero mirrored mounts the process builds no mirror queue and starts no worker.

threats.title: Mirror-write credential can be sent to a misconfigured registry target
threats.description: A mirror-write credential is a live bearer token. Under the minting tag it is minted and scoped to a domain, and under the others it is the operator's static token. If an operator could choose the write credential and the mirror-target endpoint independently, the two could diverge. They could point the mirror target at one registry while the token was minted for another. That would disclose the bearer to an endpoint that could log or replay it.
threats.mitigation: An endpoint declares its store as a tag, and the load validates the URL against that tag, so the credential and the endpoint are one declaration rather than two. Under `codeArtifact` the mint identity is parsed from the target's own host, and the tag admits no static token. Under `registry` and `verdaccio` the tag requires the operator's static token and mints nothing. The schema refuses a token key under the minting tag and a missing token key under a non-minting one, so a divergent pair is unrepresentable. Validation refuses a `codeArtifact` URL whose host is not a CodeArtifact endpoint, and on a mirror target one whose path is not the repository endpoint for the mount's own ecosystem, so a token minted for one domain reaches no other, and each refusal names the key. Two endpoints that name one registry under different tags refuse for every role, because one store has one backend, so no deployment holds two beliefs about which credential authenticates a store. An environment layer fills keys under a tag and never switches one, so a second tag on an endpoint refuses as such. The boot also refuses a mirror target that shares a host with any mount's public upstream, so the write credential cannot be aimed at a public registry. Least privilege at the store scopes the write to the intended mirror store, as defence in depth. A serve-only mount declares no mirror target and holds no mirror-write credential, so this surface does not exist there.

data.name:
Écluse Pilot
(Ingestion Pipeline)
data.description: Pilot is an unopinionated data ingestion pipeline. It fetches vulnerability data and delivers an optimised osv.db to S3. The proxy therefore never queries osv.dev on the critical path and never meets its rate limits. Pilot makes no security or blocking decision. The proxy's rules engine is the sole opinionated enforcement point. Only the rules engine evaluates that data, for example to block on CVE severity or an EPSS score, or to fast-lane a remediation package.

threats.title: Poisoned OSV payload exploits parser
threats.description: A maliciously crafted or unexpectedly massive OSV payload from upstream could cause Pilot to exhaust memory or crash during JSON parsing.
threats.mitigation: Pilot runs apart from the proxy. If Pilot runs out of memory or fails, it only delays updates. The proxy keeps serving traffic from the last-known-good osv.db snapshot.

threats.title: Pilot container-role privilege escalation
threats.description: An attacker who compromises Pilot could use its standing container credentials.
threats.mitigation: Least-privilege IAM limits the role to s3:PutObject on the one bucket prefix. Pilot runs in its own container, separate from the proxy.

threats.title: Oracle Blackout / Supply Chain DoS via OSV.dev compromise
threats.description: An attacker who gains control of osv.dev can push malicious vulnerability records. Those records trigger false positives, or fast-lane a malicious remediation package. The attack is strongest when the attacker also publishes a malicious package. Écluse explicitly trusts the OSV database as the oracle of truth.
threats.mitigation: Risk treatment: accepted by trust assumption. A compromised security oracle is a foundational supply-chain compromise. Pilot relies on OSV as a source of vulnerability truth. A hostile oracle defeats the defence outright. Transport, parsing, validation, and last-good-database controls mitigate tampering in transit, malformed payloads, and update outages. They cannot make a hostile source of truth trustworthy.

threats.title: Pathological OSV Payload (DoS)
threats.description: OSV.dev, or a compromised upstream, could serve an oversized, deeply nested, or malformed JSON file. Parsing it could exhaust CPU or memory and crash Pilot.
threats.mitigation: Pilot streams the archive and bounds each advisory as it unzips. It drains an entry past the per-advisory byte cap (8 MiB) to its boundary and drops it before it reaches the decoder. It also drops an entry whose JSON does not decode. Pilot logs and tallies both, so a few poisoned records never halt ingestion. Pilot logs an advisory that fans out into an anomalous number of ranges, and still ingests it. Deep nesting is bounded implicitly. The per-entry byte cap holds decode cost to a constant multiple of the input. Pilot also runs under the boot-resolved process heap ceiling (ECLUSE_RUNTIME__MAX_HEAP_BYTES, else cgroup memory.max). A small but deep payload therefore fails as a bounded, clean process exit rather than exhausting the machine. A systemic drop rate aborts the compile without publishing, so the proxy keeps its last-good osv.db instead of adopting a hole-ridden one. That guard reads the run's own drop tally. It fires only once at least 16 entries dropped and those drops are at least a tenth of the run, which marks a mostly unusable feed, the shape of a compromised or truncated export. Residual: an isolated depth bomb is a bounded Pilot crash rather than a per-record soft drop. A well-formed but empty or near-empty export drops nothing, so the guard passes it, and the run's row count is never read back on accept. Volumetric abuse of the fetch itself stays an operator-edge concern.

data.name: Écluse Dredger
data.description: The mirror-store pruning role of the multicall binary, run as `ecluse dredger`. It prunes already-mirrored versions that the shared rules engine now denies, on a named decisive deny that is advisory-driven or identity-driven, with no age condition. It deletes from the mirror store (Registry B) only, never the private upstream and never the publication target. It takes zero ingress and exposes only its liveness and readiness probes. It shares ecluse-core, so its rules cannot drift from the ones the serve and ingest gates run.

threats.title: Dredger inappropriately purges valid packages
threats.description: A misconfiguration in Dredger, or poisoned OSV data, could delete legitimate, needed packages from Registry B. That causes cache misses or upstream fetch failures.
threats.mitigation: Dredger must delete only from the mirror. It must delete a version only on a named decisive deny from the shared rules engine, never on deny-by-default and never while the advisory database is unavailable, because fail closed for a reaper means refusing to delete. A per-cycle deletion cap halts the cycle when a mass denial appears, which is the breaker against a poisoned advisory database. The cap's default is computed at boot as a conservative allowance per sweepable mirror store, and the configuration key raises it deliberately. The pause between sweep chunks carries a hardcoded floor the boot refuses beneath, so a mistaken sweep stays interruptible. A dry-run mode rehearses a sweep and reports what it would remove without removing it. Deletion is the backend's plain delete rather than a tombstone, so a culled version whose deny later lifts is re-admissible through the normal admission gate and the mirror behaves as a cache. A serve-only mount declares no mirrorTarget, so it holds no mirror to delete from and this surface does not exist there.

threats.title: Dredger container-role privilege escalation
threats.description: Dredger holds a standing privilege to delete from the mirror store (Registry B). An attacker who compromised Dredger could wipe that store. What bounds the privilege depends on the store. A store with its own access control can grant delete without write. A store whose only control plane is the ecosystem protocol offers no such split, so its delete runs over the same token that writes the mirror.
threats.mitigation: Dredger takes no ingress and exposes only its liveness and readiness probes. On a store with its own access control the delete credential is scoped by policy to the mirror repository alone, with no permission over the private upstream or the publication target, and a credential minted from the container role is preferred over a static secret. On a store with no such control, least privilege is an account of the store's own: a dedicated user whose package rights cover the mirror store and nothing else. The operator consent marker is deliberately distinct from the credential's capability, so holding the credential is not by itself permission to delete.

threats.title: First-party data loss from collapsed registries
threats.description: An operator can point a mount's mirrorTarget at a registry that another role already uses, such as any mount's publicationTarget or privateUpstream. Dredger deletes on a decisive deny against a mirrored public version. First-party packages and privately served packages in that same store then fall inside the blast radius.
threats.mitigation: The dredger role refuses to boot when a mount's mirrorTarget matches any mount's publicationTarget or privateUpstream by full registry URL, its own mount included. That comparison folds the authority to lower case and applies the default port, so a refusal survives a capital letter and an explicit :443, and it compares the path exactly. A mirror target on a public upstream is refused proxy-wide. Full registry URL comparison, rather than host comparison, keeps the repositories of one CodeArtifact domain apart, and it keeps a repository's per-format endpoints apart. Deletion is format-scoped. Only the vetting pass issues the cleared backend that builds the delete capability. A refusal from any of its rules fails the whole pass, so an overlapping configuration cannot reach a delete at all. One combinator turns each detected collision into the outcome the booting role earns, so a refusal and a warning cannot describe different rules. The proxy and the mirror worker boot on a collapsed pair, and each warns once for it. Collapsing the registries deliberately surrenders Dredger's automated pruning.

threats.title: Accidental permanent deletion of registry data
threats.description: Dredger issues permanent hard deletions against the mirror registry. Misconfigured, or pointed at the wrong registry, it destroys data permanently.
threats.mitigation: Dredger verifies explicit operator consent before any destructive action, and again at the start of every cycle. Consent is read through the store backend's own maintenance handle, never through the ecosystem adapter, because the marker is a fact of the store and not of the protocol it speaks. Its form is fixed per tag. A `codeArtifact` store carries a resource tag on the repository, key `ecluse-dredger-consent`, value `true`, read with a read-only permission. A `verdaccio` store carries `permitDeletion: true` under the tag in the mount's own configuration. Withdrawing the `codeArtifact` tag halts the next cycle without a restart. The `verdaccio` key is read at boot, so withdrawing that one takes a restart. A `registry` store has no consent form and no control plane, so the Dredger refuses it at boot and names the tag. Consent fails closed. An absent, unreadable, or errored marker refuses that store, and the refusal logs the backend's own descriptor telling the operator how to attach consent. Consent is deliberately distinct from the credential's capability, so holding a credential that can delete is not by itself permission to delete. The dredger role also refuses to boot when a mount's mirrorTarget matches any mount's privateUpstream, or its own mount's publicationTarget, by full registry URL. Every role refuses a mirror target on another mount's publicationTarget. The per-cycle deletion cap latches: reaching it stops the Dredger for the life of the process, so a poisoned advisory generation cannot be swept again by a supervisor restart. A dry run builds the role with no real delete in it, so a rehearsal cannot delete because nothing it holds can. A version is deleted only on a named decisive deny; deny by default, a version the store's own metadata no longer carries, and a version that could not be vetted all keep.

threats.title: Massive Purge DoS
threats.description: A bug in Dredger, or a malicious rule configuration, could fire thousands of deletion requests at once. That exhausts the registry API limits and denies service to the private mirror.
threats.mitigation: The default cycle carries only the package names the advisory database covers or an identity-deny rule pins, so the destructive calls one cycle can make are bounded by advisory hits rather than by store size. It sweeps in chunks, with a configured pause between them. A store fault is retried once after the delay the fault itself advises, and a fault that survives that retry halts the cycle. A per-cycle deletion cap halts the sweep for the life of the process, which bounds any single runaway sweep.

threats.title: Configured deletion consent stays valid when the store it names changes
threats.description: Consent to delete is a marker on the store itself, so pointing the Dredger at a store nobody consented for fails the check. The `verdaccio` tag carries consent as `permitDeletion: true`, a key in the mount's own configuration, so it travels with the deployment rather than with the store. An operator who re-points the `verdaccio:` mirror target at a different Verdaccio store keeps a configuration that still says yes, and the Dredger reads consent for a store nobody granted it for. The same key carries the store's classification, so a re-pointed target is also read as standalone.
threats.mitigation: Risk treatment: accepted as a development-store exception, 2026-09-04. Verdaccio is a development and test store, and nobody runs a package proxy in front of a package proxy in production, so the exception is bounded to that tag and exists on no other. Verdaccio serves no marker a protocol read could carry, and no protocol read can see whether such a store refills itself from an uplink, so the operator's own key is the only evidence either way and consent and classification are one key. The collision refusal is the misdirection guard that remains. The dredger role refuses to boot when a mount's mirrorTarget matches any mount's privateUpstream, or its own mount's publicationTarget, by full registry URL, and every role refuses two endpoints that name one registry under different tags. Every role refuses a mirror target on another mount's publicationTarget. Residual: a re-pointed `verdaccio:` target that collides with no other declared endpoint still carries consent, and the Dredger deletes from it.

data.name: delete pruned versions
data.description: Dredger issues delete requests to Registry B based on the versions the shared rules engine denies, advisory-driven or identity-driven.

threats.title: Store-supplied path components steer a credential-bearing delete
threats.description: Removing one version from a protocol-only store is an edit over the store's own package document. Écluse reads that document, takes the revision marker and the artifact's file name out of it, puts the revision into the URLs of a `PUT` and a `DELETE`, and the file name into the `DELETE`, both carrying the mirror-write token. Écluse authored neither value, and a publisher supplies the tarball location the file name is taken from. A component holding a separator, a dot-dot, or a control character could steer either request at another path on the store.
threats.mitigation: Both components parse against the same deny-by-default component gate the serve path applies, which refuses an empty component, a bare dot or dot-dot, and any component holding a slash, a backslash, or a control character. A file name that fails the gate falls back to the conventional name built from the package and the version, and a revision marker that fails it refuses that one version rather than forming a request. The build then percent-encodes every component it interpolates and keeps only the unreserved set verbatim, so safety rests on encode-on-build and not on the gate alone. Every request is formed against the store's own base URL, which is https-only with certificate validation, and it reaches the wire sealed with the redirect count pinned to zero, so no hop can move a credential-bearing write after the request is formed. The document is read under the response-size bound, so an oversized answer ends the read. Residual: the gate is structural, so a name that is a valid component but not the version's own artifact still forms a delete against this one store, bounded by the mirror store the credential reaches.
